Usage: dotnet decompile <assembly> [<assembly> ...] [options]

Writes the C# of a .NET assembly. Without --output the C# goes to standard
output. Each assembly, and each type named by --type, becomes one file, so
a run that writes more than one needs a directory.

An <assembly> is a file, a directory, or a pattern. A directory reads every
.dll, .exe and .winmd in it. A pattern takes * and ? within a name, and **
for any depth of directories, as in bin/**/*.dll. Quote a pattern so the
shell leaves it to this tool. Files a pattern finds below other directories
keep that path under --output, and so do assemblies that would otherwise
share a file, below the directory they have in common.

Options:
  -o, --output <path>     Write to this file, or into this directory when it
                          already exists, ends with a separator, or the run
                          writes more than one file.
  -t, --type <full name>  Write only this top level type. Repeat to name
                          several. With several assemblies, each one's
                          types go in a directory named as its own file
                          would be, without the .cs.
      --list-types        List the top level types and stop. With several
                          assemblies, each one's list follows the last.
  -r, --reference <dir>   Also look here for the assemblies this one
                          references. Repeat to name several.
      --                  Read everything after this as an assembly,
                          even where it starts with a dash.
      --no-bodies         Write signatures without method bodies.
      --no-keywords       Write System.Int32 where int would do.
      --block-namespaces  Wrap each namespace in braces.
      --indent <n|tab>    Indent with n spaces, or with a tab. Default 4.
      --newline <lf|crlf> End lines this way. Default lf.
      --lang-version <latest|preview>
                          Write C# for this language version. Preview
                          spells clo
